name: Truth-default theory
statement: People passively presume that what others tell them is honest, and abandon that presumption only when something triggers suspicion.
meaning: Two claims travel under this heading and they are not the same claim. Truth-bias is a measurement: the proportion of messages a judge calls honest when a researcher asks. The truth-default is a claim about what happens when nobody asks, namely that the possibility of deception does not come to mind at all. Levine's theory joins them to a third idea, that the default is worth having. If most of what people hear is honest, believing it produces correct beliefs most of the time, and the cost of checking every utterance is higher than the cost of the lies that get through. Around that core sit a set of separate modules, each with its own evidence: that a few prolific liars tell most lies, that accuracy is higher for truths than for lies, that accuracy tracks the truth-lie base rate in a straight line, that some senders look honest whatever they are doing, and that lies are caught through evidence and confession rather than through reading behaviour. The theory is a package, and the parts have been tested to very different depths.

origin.where: Journal of Language and Social Psychology
origin.note: The article calls itself an initial sketch. It defines the truth-default as a passive presumption of honesty, arising either from never considering deceit or from falling back after failing to find evidence of it, and sets out the theory's modules and propositions. Levine credits the older observation that people are truth-biased to McCornack and Parks and to Zuckerman and colleagues, and says what is new is the argument that the presumption is adaptive rather than a flaw.

evidence: Bond and DePaulo's meta-analysis pooled 206 documents and 24,483 judges, covering 6,651 messages from 4,435 senders. Across 292 receiver samples the unweighted mean was 53.98% correct, and weighted methods gave 53.46%, 95% confidence interval 53.31% to 53.59%. Their own wording is that 54% is a reasonable estimate for the grand mean. The split behind the average carries more information than the average. In 207 samples, judges classified 61.34% of truthful messages correctly and 47.55% of deceptive ones. Receivers called 56.86% of messages honest on unweighted analysis and 55.23% weighted, 95% confidence interval 54.99% to 55.46%. Across studies the proportion of truth judgements was unrelated to the proportion correct, r = -.008. Levine, Kim, Park and Hughes tested the Park-Levine model against point predictions. Fifty participants judged interviews at an even base rate: they called 66.1% of messages true, got 67.1% of truths and 34.3% of lies right, and scored 50.7% overall, which did not beat chance. A separate 413 participants were assigned to eight base rates running from no honest messages to all of them. Accuracy rose with the proportion of honest messages, eta-squared .24 for the induction, slope 0.316, and the deviation from a straight line was not significant. Predictions built from the first group's truth and lie accuracy correlated .97 with the eight obtained means and missed them by 2.6 percentage points on average, the largest miss being 4.5 points. Levine, Park and McCornack's own third study, read here off the scan, recruited 177 students and analysed 174. Accuracy was 59.48% where 75% of messages were honest, 51.88% at 50% and 39.83% at 25%. Clare and Levine ran two experiments in which thought-listing came before or after a prompted truth-lie judgement, one with video and one face to face. Absent prior prompting, receivers mentioned the veracity of what they had heard less than 10% of the time. Serota, Levine and Boster asked 1,000 US adults how many lies they had told in a day. Sixty percent reported none, and almost half of all reported lies came from 5% of respondents.

examples.tag: The reason given for a missed delivery
examples.text: A courier explains a missed slot by saying the van broke down, and the customer reschedules without once weighing whether it is true. The possibility of a lie is not considered and rejected. It never comes up at all.

examples.tag: A new colleague's account of an old job
examples.text: Over lunch someone describes the work they used to do, and the listener files all of it as fact. Checking every claim would cost far more than the occasional false one gets through, which is the argument for the default.

A friend's account of his weekend contradicts a photograph seen the day before, and only then does the listener start weighing everything else he said. Suspicion needed a trigger, and until the trigger came nothing was being assessed.

replication.headline: The truth bias and the veracity effect hold in a large independent reanalysis, which at the same time found no trace of the sender differences the theory uses to explain low accuracy.
replication.detail: Volz, Reinhard and Müller reanalysed four lie-detection studies built on the Miami University Deception Detection Database, in which each sender supplied several truthful and several deceptive messages. Across 45,691 judgements from 2,903 judges, 12 of whom were dropped from the models, truth bias ran higher than in the meta-analysis, at 69.12% of messages judged honest, and mean accuracy ran lower, at 50.99%. Truth accuracy again exceeded lie accuracy, and message veracity was the best predictor of whether a judgement was correct. The sender-level claims did not survive. Messages differed in detectability, 21% of variance, of which veracity accounted for 16.8% of the total, while senders did not differ across their messages, and the distribution of sender detectability showed no sign of the transparent liars the theory posits. Judges drove the variance in whether a message was called a lie, put at 12% in the abstract and 16% in the discussion, and 46% of the variance in confidence. Their share of accuracy was under 0.01%. Halevy, Shalvi and Verschuere found most people reporting little or no lying, with self-reported frequent lying correlating with real cheating and psychopathic tendency, which puts the prolific-liar pattern outside Levine's group. Sánchez, Masip and Herrero had participants log every lie they noticed over ten weeks and found non-behavioural information more useful than behavioural cues, in line with the theory's content-in-context claim. The high-accuracy questioning results are the thin part of the record. Levine's own test in South Korea, n = 81, pushed accuracy to 65% and down to 30% by varying how the interviewee was questioned. Vrij, Meissner and Kassin argue that theoretical and methodological features of those experiments undermine the reliability and validity of the data, that the studies therefore add nothing meaningful to the literatures on lie detection and false confessions, and that the results are dangerously misleading. Levine and Blair's reply reports accuracy over 95% by expert interrogators in both experiments and 87 of 89 interviews called correctly in the second, and grants that until the findings are replicated by other researchers and labs, caution is scientifically warranted.

study.cite: Volz, S., Reinhard, M.-A., & Müller, P. (2023). Is it the judge, the sender, or just the individual message? Disentangling person and message effects on variation in lie-detection judgments. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 18(6), 1368-1387.

limits: The base-rate model's point-prediction test and every published follow-up come from Levine's own group. Crossref lists an interactive base-rate experiment in 2014 and a Korean replication in 2017, both with Levine or Park on the byline, and a 2015 critique by Burgoon with a reply from Park and Levine. None of those four was read here. The Volz reanalysis rests on a single stimulus database. Its authors note that people uneasy about being filmed, or about lying on camera, may never have taken part, which would compress the sender variance they went looking for. Two claims are quoted at one remove. Levine and Serota's reanalysis is quoted from the abstract deposited at Crossref. OpenAlex and Unpaywall both list the article as open at Sage, but on 21 September 2026 Sage answered every route with a Cloudflare bot challenge rather than a paywall. Halevy, Shalvi and Verschuere are quoted from the abstract published at Oxford Academic, which gives neither a sample size nor a correlation. One source was not read at all. Fan, Griffin and Tagg's test of trigger sensitivity in intergroup communication sits behind the same Cloudflare challenge at Taylor and Francis, carries no abstract at Crossref, and on 21 September 2026 had no copy listed at OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar or Europe PMC. One figure has been read as a mismatch and is not one. Levine's 2022 review describes accuracy in these experiments as normally distributed around 54% with a standard deviation of about 6%. That is Bond and DePaulo's observed 6.11%, which is the spread of study means rather than of judges, and from which they infer a true across-study value of 4.52%.
misreadings: The 54% is quoted as the accuracy of human lie detection. It is the grand mean of experiments in which half the messages were lies, and the weighted estimate in the same paper is 53.46%. Levine and Serota's reanalysis reports truth bias correlating .88 with accuracy for truths, -.88 with accuracy for lies and below .03 with overall accuracy, and argues that the 54% claim needs contextualising. The second misreading runs the other way, treating truth bias as a documented failure of judgement. The argument here is that where most messages are honest, believing them is right most of the time, which is a claim about base rates rather than about credulity. A third is treating truth-bias scores as measurements of the truth-default. Truth-bias is what a prompted judge does; the truth-default is the claim that the question does not arise unprompted, and the figure that measures it is the under-10% from Clare and Levine, produced in the theory's own laboratory. The sender demeanour work is over-read in the same way. Its headline, that varying senders explained between 59% and 98% of the variance in detection accuracy, describes senders the experimenters had selected so that demeanour and honesty were matched or mismatched. It is not an estimate of how much ordinary senders differ, and the largest independent test of that question found they do not.
